description: Team LUNARES is building AstroSynapse-X, a health-gated autonomous landing and rover system for lunar missions. Already field-tested in Poland and patent-pending in India. We work across embedded hardware, AI/ML, and systems design. Looking for teammates skilled in hardware prototyping, sensor integration, or dashboard development who want to build something real.
summary:
When astronauts fly to Mars, a radio message to Earth can take anywhere from 3 to 22 minutes to arrive. If something goes wrong with their health, they can't just call a doctor and get an answer right away like they could on the Space Station. They have to handle a lot of it themselves.

We built LANDFALL to help with that. It's an app that runs on the spaceship, even without internet. Every day it checks the astronaut's sleep, heart rate, blood pressure, mood and the air inside the cabin, and compares them with what's normal for that specific person. It also predicts how fit they'll be when they land on Mars, using NASA's research on bone and muscle loss in space.

When something looks off, LANDFALL decides who should deal with it: the astronaut themselves, the crew's medical officer, or a doctor back on Earth. That depends on how far away Earth is that day. Reports to Earth are saved and sent automatically once the connection comes back, so nothing gets lost. A 3D model of the astronaut's body shows exactly where the problems are.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Every day of a 180-day trip to Mars, LANDFALL goes through the same five steps.

1. Read. It collects the astronaut's sleep, heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, mood and exercise, plus the CO2 level and radiation inside the ship.

2. Detect. It compares today's numbers with that astronaut's own normal, which it learns during the first 14 days. So if someone usually sleeps 7.4 hours and suddenly gets 4.2, the app notices, especially if it keeps happening.

3. Forecast. It predicts how ready the astronaut will be on landing day in six areas: bones, muscles, heart, balance, sleep and mood. The bone and muscle numbers come from NASA's Human Research Program. You can move an exercise slider and see how working out more or less changes the result. Each area gets a simple GO, WATCH or NO-GO.

4. Decide. It works out who should handle the problem: the astronaut, the crew's medical officer, or a flight surgeon on Earth. This depends on how serious it is, whether a medical officer is on board, and how far away Earth is that day. If Earth is close enough, it suggests a live call. If not, it sends a written report. The app always explains why it made the decision and what would change it. Real emergencies skip the queue completely.

5. Deliver. The report is packed into a message with a checksum, which is like a fingerprint that proves nothing got corrupted on the way. If the connection to Earth is down, the message waits and sends itself automatically once the link is back.

WHAT YOU SEE

The website looks like a spaceship control screen. It has live health cards with 14-day trends, a readiness score, today’s decision with the reasons behind it, and a panel showing messages waiting to be sent to Earth with a countdown for the radio delay.

In the middle is a 3D hologram of the astronaut’s body. You can rotate it, click any body part to zoom in, switch to an X-ray view to see the skeleton, or turn on a heat map that shows which areas are getting weaker. The heart beats at the astronaut’s actual heart rate for that day. You can also zoom from the whole body down to tissue layers and even a close-up of the bone structure.

A slider lets you jump to any day of the mission, and a 40-second demo walks through a story where the astronaut’s sleep suddenly collapses on day 40.

We also built a gamified version of the dashboard to make it easier and more engaging for anyone to explore. It turns the health data into a mission briefing where you earn points for catching risk signals early, unlock new body systems as you investigate deeper, and get a mission score at the end based on how well you kept the crew safe. The idea is that a doctor, a student, or even a curious viewer can all understand what is happening to the astronaut’s body without needing a medical background

WHY IT MATTERS

On a Mars mission, the crew can’t rely on Earth for quick medical help. LANDFALL gives them clear advice they can trust, because every rule is visible instead of hidden inside a black box. It also makes sure health reports reach Earth even when the connection drops, and it works completely offline.

Right now, astronaut health data is scattered across different systems and specialists back on Earth. A flight surgeon might miss an early warning sign simply because they are looking at one number in isolation. LANDFALL pulls everything together into one view, connects the dots between sleep, bone density, heart rate, and cognitive load, and flags a risk before it becomes a crisis. That kind of early warning could be the difference between catching a problem in week two and dealing with an emergency in week fourteen.

There is also a training gap. Most mission health tools are built for specialists. A crew member with no medical background has to trust a recommendation they cannot verify. LANDFALL changes that by showing the reasoning behind every alert in plain language, so the astronaut on duty can understand why the system is saying what it says and push back if something feels wrong. That transparency builds trust, and trust is what gets a crew to actually follow the advice when it counts.

The same system works for Earth too. Remote research stations in Antarctica, offshore drilling platforms, and disaster response teams all face the same problem: medical expertise is hours away and the connection is unreliable. LANDFALL was built for the harshest environment imaginable, which means it transfers directly to any situation where you need a doctor but cannot have one.

HOW WE BUILT IT

The frontend is a pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application with no build step or framework dependency, which keeps it lightweight and easy to deploy in environments where package managers and build pipelines are not available. The 3D anatomical model is rendered in real time using Three.js, with custom shader materials, a lathe-geometry body rig, and a beating heart animation tied to the astronaut’s actual heart rate data. All health trend charts use Chart.js with a consistent design system across every panel.

A service worker caches all assets on first load so the entire application runs fully offline. This was a hard requirement from the start, since any Mars or deep-space deployment cannot assume a reliable connection to update resources on demand.

On the data side, we built an experimental health forecasting module in Python using NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn. It processes the NASA Open Science Data Repository biomedical datasets and outputs risk predictions that feed into the decision engine on the dashboard.

To keep the codebase reliable under time pressure, we wrote 48 unit tests covering the core logic and a separate smoke test suite that verifies all 16 primary features are present and functional on every build. Both suites run automatically through GitHub Actions on every push, so a broken change never reaches the live site without being flagged first. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages and the full source is open.

Code repository: https://github.com/omaggarwal-2006/astrix

THINGS WE WERE CAREFUL ABOUT

The whole idea is built around the delay. The same symptom needs a different response when Earth is 3 seconds away than when it's 20 minutes away. We never show a status using colour alone; it always comes with a shape and a word, so it's readable for colour-blind users too. Every number either comes from a NASA source or is clearly marked as our own assumption. All astronaut data in the demo is made up, and LANDFALL is meant to support decisions, not replace a doctor.

TEAM

Raghav Dua worked on the decision rules, the message system, testing and documentation.

Tanishk built the health detection, the forecasts, the machine learning model and the sample data.

Om built the user interface, the mission scene, the 3D body and offline support.

Rohan designed the look of the website, creating the visual mockups for every screen that the final interface is based on.

Parth researched the NASA sources and space health data behind our numbers and helped prepare the presentation and demo.
